dsh-search

中文

A real result page, not an account balance.

A DeepSeek Harness profile bundle that gives the web_search tool a search backend which needs no API key, no account balance and no model call. It registers both halves of the web seam: bing-html searches Bing's public result page, and article hands web_fetch a page's prose instead of its markup. Search keeps working when the account behind the shipped provider has run out — the failure that makes chat work and every search fail — and a fetched page costs the context its article rather than its navigation.

github.com/FrozenYty/dsh-search

Status

  • Current version: v0.4.1.
  • Verified here: the parser over two saved result pages, the request shape over a stubbed request layer, and a mutation scan that breaks each load-bearing line of bing.js and requires a test to notice — node --test, node scripts/mutation-scan.mjs and node scripts/check.mjs, all recorded with their output in PROGRESS.md. The live search was run by hand against cn.bing.com and answered with real sources; that run and its output are in PROGRESS.md too.
  • Exercised in a real profile: installed into a desktop profile on 2026-11-13, and web_search returned eight live sources in a session whose chat runs through a relay while the DeepSeek account balance is zero — the case this bundle exists for. The install output, and why it is that provider serving the call, are recorded in PROGRESS.md.
  • Not automatic: scripts/check.mjs and the tests never load the Harness, so the live check above is a manual step each time. Nothing in this repository can show that the plugin activates in your profile.
  • Release list: CHANGELOG.md. Append-only history: PROGRESS.md.

Install and verify

Two routes, and both put the same bundle into a profile and apply its patch. Neither needs a build step and neither touches the npm registry: for a project this size the working tree is the distribution — clone it, install that path, and git pull is the update.

From the Harness — ask for this directory to be installed:

plugin_manager  install_bundle  target: <absolute path to this repository>

From the CLI, with the same local path — the route the rest of the plugin ecosystem documents:

dsh plugin --profile <profile> add <absolute path to this repository>

Nothing is published, and a linked working tree picks up a git pull on the next load — that is the whole update story. To hand it to a friend, send them the repository: git clone, or Code → Download ZIP, which is already installable because nothing here needs a build. They install that folder with either route above, restart the app, and the plugin list shows 搜索.

That this package is not on npm is deliberate: the name dsh-search there belongs to an unrelated package, and this one is private — it is linked or installed from a file, never published (docs/adr/0003-provider-id-and-plugin-name.md).

Whichever route you use, the patch moves the web seam's searchProvider to bing-html and restates the row's fetch half. That is the part that makes the provider selected, and it changes the profile for every session in it — see below.

Verification afterwards is live calls, not check output:

  • the patch applies with no warning about the rows it targets, and the plugin inventory lists this bundle with the title 搜索 (or Search in an English UI);
  • ask a question that needs the web in a session whose chat goes through a relay while the DeepSeek account balance is still zero. web_search should return sources with absolute URLs, where it used to fail with an HTTP 402 from api.deepseek.com;
  • the failure that proves it was this provider, not the shipped one: a search no longer mentions api.deepseek.com, and fetching one of the returned URLs with web_fetch returns the page's prose — what this bundle's article provider extracts — instead of its navigation.

To stop using it, override the same row in the profile's own cordis.patch.yml — that layer is applied after this bundle's, so it wins:

- id: web
  config:
    searchProvider: deepseek-official
    fetchProvider: http

How it works

One search is one HTTPS GET to https://cn.bing.com/search?q=…, and the response body is parsed for its organic result blocks. Each block contributes a title, an absolute URL and a snippet, plus the publication date when the page states one — lifted out of the snippet and normalised, because the seam carries it as its own field and the tool shows it as metadata. The seam caps the list at the caller's maxResults. Nothing is sent to an account, nothing is billed, and no model call is involved.

The request never touches any other host. www.bing.com redirects to cn.bing.com, and this provider sets redirect: "manual", so a redirect is never followed — it becomes an error naming its target instead. scripts/check.mjs asserts at the request layer that one search sends exactly one request, to cn.bing.com, and never to www.bing.com or api.deepseek.com.

Choosing who searches

A profile with this bundle has two searches available: the keyless one it registers, and the shipped deepseek-official provider, whose credential the profile may still carry. The choice is yours, and it is one field on this bundle's row:

- id: search   # `web-search-bing-html` before 0.2.0 (ADR 0007)
  config:
    provider: keyless   # keyless (default) | official | auto
  • keyless — Bing's result page: no account, no key, no balance. The default, and what every earlier version did.
  • official — the shipped provider serves the search, billed to the same account as the chat. If it is not registered, or registered and unable to run, the search fails with the seam's own code (WEB_PROVIDER_CONFIGURED_MISSING / WEB_PROVIDER_CONFIGURED_UNAVAILABLE) and a message naming the provider you asked for: a deliberate choice should not quietly become a different one.
  • auto — the shipped provider when it can run, keyless otherwise. A failing account is remembered for the rest of the process, so a zero balance costs one doomed request rather than one per search.

Measured on this machine the account sits at -0.09 CNY with is_available: false, so keyless and auto are the modes that answer today and official becomes useful the moment the balance is topped up.

A profile can also take this bundle out of the path entirely by overriding the seam's own row in its cordis.patch.yml — that layer is applied after a bundle's, so it wins:

- id: web
  config:
    searchProvider: deepseek-official
    fetchProvider: http

That is the blunter instrument: no auto, and this bundle's error messages go with it. Both switches are one line; the difference is whether you want the fallback.

The other half: web_fetch

The seam has two halves, and this bundle owns both: bing-html searches, article fetches. The patch pins fetchProvider: article while it overrides the web row — the seam replaces a row's config wholesale, so without that line the fetch half would fall back to auto-selection.

Why a provider of its own: the shipped http provider hands over a page's markup, chrome and all. Measured on five real pages, 61 % of the characters were chrome by a lower bound (script, style, nav, header, footer, aside, comments) and prose inside <p> was 1.4 % of what arrived; on three of the five the shipped provider's 100 000-character body cap was reached before the article began, so the tail was never read and no transformation of what arrived could recover it. The article provider therefore reads the page itself, with the shipped provider's own numbers (its User-Agent, same-origin redirects only, a 5 MB read cap, the charset the response declares), extracts the prose, and hands over text — which the tool passes through instead of running its own markdown pass (docs/adr/0010-the-other-half-of-the-result.md).

It is a rule, not a readability engine: remove the containers that are never prose, drop navigation lists and tables whose words are the anchors' words — unless the block carries a paragraph, which is content whatever its link density — keep headings, paragraphs, quotations, code and tables in document order, and say so when it caps at 24 000 characters — a truncated page that looks complete is worse than one that says it was cut. A redirect that changes origin is reported instead of followed, naming the target; a non-2xx answer is a result, not a throw.

The User-Agent is one decision for the whole bundle, and it is the honest one. Measured across six real pages, a desktop Chrome disguise was not an improvement:

Host Product UA (shipped) Desktop Chrome UA
zhuanlan.zhihu.com 403 — Zhihu's own block 403, unchanged
blog.csdn.net 200, 317 kB 521, 2 kB — worse
juejin.cn, developer.aliyun.com, github.com, deepseekharness.online 200 200

So the default stays: a browser disguise wins nothing here and loses CSDN's whole page, and the sites the shipped provider cannot fetch are ones whose anti-bot rejects a sessionless client whatever it claims to be. web_fetch reports the status it actually got, which is the honest answer to give a model.

The one composition change

Registering a provider is not enough to be selected. The shipped base bundle pins the seam's searchProvider to deepseek-official and its fetchProvider to http, so this bundle's patch moves both pins and restates the row's every field — the seam replaces a row's config wholesale, never merges it, so both lines have to be written out again or that half would lose its backend.

That is the whole footprint: one row override and one inserted row. It changes the profile the bundle is installed into, for every session in it, which is why it is stated here rather than buried in the patch.

Limits and deliberate omissions

  • One engine, one endpoint, and that is a measurement rather than a shortcut. Bing's HTML result page is the only backend that answers this machine with parseable, directly-linkable results: Google, DuckDuckGo, Brave and a SearXNG instance are unreachable here, Mojeek answers 403, Sogou redirects to itself, 360 wraps every result in a redirect web_fetch will not follow, and Baidu starts answering with a captcha after about eight requests. docs/adr/0004-one-backend-measured.md has the table; node scripts/probe-backends.mjs re-asks the network whenever it may have changed.

  • A markup change is a real risk. The parser reads a page, not an API. A page that stops matching it fails with no parseable result block instead of quietly returning nothing, and the saved fixtures under tests/fixtures/ are how that shows up as a failing test rather than as a mystery.

  • One page, about ten results, and that is this endpoint's ceiling. No paging, no retries — and not for lack of trying. Measured three ways: every offset and count returns page one's ten results (count=20/30/50, first=11/21/31, the page's own "next" link with its FPIG hash, the same with the set-cookie values from the first response sent back and a Referer), Bing's RSS form (&format=rss) carries ten items and ignores count and first alike, and the runs used broad queries (python tutorial, 中国 历史) so a small result set could not be mistaken for a paging failure. The fetch half does not retry either, and that was measured the day after two unexplained transport failures: 50 requests across five hosts returned 0 transport failures, and retrying a failure nobody can reproduce would be code nothing protects. The same run did find that blog.csdn.net answers non-2xx 9 times out of 10 when requested in a loop — an anti-bot behaving normally, and the reason a non-2xx answer comes back as a result instead of a throw.

  • What widens a call is the tool's own caps — when the layer that owns the row lets you set them. One web_search merges up to searchMaxQueries queries (default 4) into at most searchMaxResults sources (default 8). Both live on the base bundle's tool-web row, and a profile can raise them — restating the row's other fields, because a patch replaces its config wholesale:

    - id: tool-web
  config:
    fetch: true
    searchTimeoutMs: 60000
    searchMaxResults: 24

    A later patch layer that restates the same row replaces its config too, and the value falls back to the default without a word. A desktop profile does exactly that: the app's own preset patch restates tool-web with fetch and searchTimeoutMs only, so the snippet above composes correctly — the loader's own composeEntries over that profile's layers resolves it to 24 — and the tool still measures 8. What works in that situation is the question rather than the cap: two or three sub-queries in one call are what widen the net, and a second web_search call is how to see more.

  • A page parsed in the last five minutes answers again. Five minutes, at most 32 pages, the least-recently-used one evicted first, and a failure never kept — a challenge page wants a retry, not a memory of being blocked (docs/adr/0008-reusing-a-recent-page.md). It is the one case where a search costs no request; every other clause in this list still holds.

    A profile reads its patch when it loads, so a running Host keeps the old number until it restarts — unless its package.json sets dsh.profile.patchReload: live, in which case the file is watched. How to tell which cap is live: the tool appends (Showing the first N sources…) only when the seam truncated, so that line disappearing is the change taking effect.

  • A result link that Bing wraps in its own redirect (cn.bing.com/ck/a?…) would be returned as that wrapper URL rather than unwrapped. It has not happened once in 80 measured results, so the parser does not unwrap; PLAN.md records the measurement.

  • Query operators are hints, not filters. Measured on this endpoint: site:github.com alone was honoured on all ten results, site:github.com dsh on one and site:github.com dsh plugin on two; intitle: and quotation marks changed nothing measurable. Write the query you mean and treat an operator as a nudge, not a guarantee.

  • No domain filter. The seam's search request carries a query and a result bound, nothing else, so a provider cannot receive allowed_domains/blocked_domains-style filters — that is a limit of where this sits, not of the engine. Writing site: into the query works only when the query is nothing but the operator (measured; see above).

  • The fetch half is a rule, not a readability engine. It removes containers that are never prose and navigation lists, keeps the rest in document order, and caps at 24 000 characters with a marker. A page it reads badly is a bug report with a fixture, not a tuning session; docs/adr/0010-the-other-half-of-the-result.md says what was deliberately not built.

  • No data directory. This bundle writes nothing: no cache on disk, no index, no state that could move when the repository or the profile does. node scripts/check.mjs prints that answer on every run, and docs/adr/0011-no-data-directory.md says where a future one would have to go — ~/.agents/search, resolved per use, never at load.

  • No settings, no timers, no background work. There is nothing to configure and nothing running when a search is not in flight.

When it stops working

Bing will change its result page eventually. The provider fails loudly rather than answering with nothing, and its message names the failure, so the first step is to read it:

  • no parseable result block … shape may have changed — the markup moved. Run node scripts/fixture-refresh.mjs: it re-fetches the three pages the fixtures came from through this provider's own request, reports what each one parses to now, and exits non-zero when a page yields fewer sources than its stored fixture. Once you have read the page and know the parser is right, --write saves it and re-dates the provenance table.
  • challenge page instead of results — Bing decided this client looked automated. Retry later, or open the same query in a browser once; the provider keeps no session and no cookie.
  • HTTP 302 … redirects to https://www.bing.com/… — the routing changed. That is a decision point, not a bug: ADR 0001 says a redirect is never followed, so supersede that ADR rather than flipping the flag.
  • Bing search request failed: — the request never completed. That one is the network, not the parser.

npm run acceptance sends one real request and prints what came back, which is the quickest way to see that message outside a session. It needs the network and nothing else.

Development

npm install                       # the seam the entry tests load; the bundle installs nothing itself
node --check index.js bing.js article.js
node --test --test-isolation=none tests/*.test.mjs
node scripts/mutation-scan.mjs
node scripts/check.mjs

npm install is for the entry tests alone: index.js imports the seam, which a linked bundle receives from the runtime as a declared peer, and those tests load the real class rather than a stand-in. Without it they skip — and a skip means the entry is unverified, which is why scripts/check.mjs fails when CI stops installing it. Everything else in the suite runs with no install at all.

--test-isolation=none is not optional: Node 22 spells it --experimental-test-isolation, so the flag itself fixes the major version at Node 24, and the default runner spawns one process per test file, which this machine's sandbox refuses. CI pins Node 24 and runs the same commands, so a local pass is the same statement as a green run.

The mutation scan is what keeps the suite honest: for each load-bearing line of bing.js it applies one mutation and requires at least one test to fail. A survivor is a line nothing protects, and it fails the build with the mutation's name.

Nothing is published, so there is no release step either: the gate above is the whole delivery. A version number moves only when the bundle's own files change — the ones files lists — and CONTRIBUTING.md §5 says which those are.

The manual acceptance run is the one thing the gate cannot do for you: it needs the network, and the session check needs the plugin enabled.

Repository layout

Path What
index.js Bundle entry: builds the provider and registers it with ctx.web
bing.js The query, the request, the parse and the result mapping; imports nothing
article.js The fetch half: reads a page itself and extracts its prose; imports only bing.js
cordis.patch.yml The seam pin and this bundle's row
tests/ Parsing tests over two saved result pages, and request-layer tests over a stubbed fetch
scripts/check.mjs The repository gate, including the two request-layer regressions
docs/ The design document (bilingual) and the ADRs
PLAN.md, PROGRESS.md, CHANGELOG.md Acceptance state, the append-only record, release summaries
locale/, icon.svg, package.json The bundle's inventory half
.github/workflows/ ci.yml, the gate a change must pass; drift.yml, the weekly re-check of the saved pages
